task.title: Study Forensics: Four-day workweek trial improves well-being
task.prompt: A six-month experiment across 141 companies in six countries tested whether cutting the work week from five days to four while maintaining pay could improve employee well-being. Companies volunteered to restructure their workflows so that productivity would not decline with fewer hours. Nearly 2,900 participants completed surveys before and after the trial. After six months, workers reported lower stress and burnout, higher job satisfaction, and no perceived drop in performance. More than 90 percent of participating companies chose to continue the four-day schedule. The researchers cautioned that because companies self-selected into the trial and outcomes were self-reported, further randomised evaluations are needed.
task.context:
A large multi-company trial with positive results but important methodological
limitations (self-selection, self-report). The researchers acknowledge limitations openly.
task.reference_solution: The summary reports results from a large multi-company trial showing improvements in employee well-being without apparent productivity loss. It notes limitations such as voluntary participation and self-reported outcomes. Although the study design has weaknesses, the claims are restrained to measured outcomes and the need for further research is acknowledged.

task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent recognise honest reporting of limited evidence without overflagging?
task.gold_summary: The summary reports results from a large multi-company trial of a four-day workweek showing improvements in well-being without productivity loss. It notes limitations such as voluntary participation and self-reported outcomes.

gold_evidence_spans.span: workers reported lower stress and burnout, higher job satisfaction, and no perceived drop in performance
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Directly supports the claim that the four-day schedule improved well-being.

gold_evidence_spans.span: researchers cautioned that because companies self-selected into the trial and outcomes were self-reported, further randomised evaluations are needed
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Explicit acknowledgement of methodological limitations represents honest uncertainty.

task.gold_justification:
Although the study was not randomised and relies on self-report, the summary accurately
conveys the evidence and includes caveats. The claims are restrained to the measured
outcomes, and the need for further research is acknowledged. The self-selection bias
weakens the evidence but the authors are transparent about it. We label this solid
because the reporting matches the evidence quality — no overclaim is made.
task.gold_alternative_reading:
Some may argue that self-selection (only enthusiastic companies participated) and
self-reported outcomes (workers may overstate satisfaction) limit the evidence quality
enough to warrant an overclaim label. The 90% continuation rate may reflect commitment
bias rather than objective success. A reasonable analyst could mark this as borderline
overclaim due to the design limitations.
task.curator_notes:
Key borderline case. The evidence is real but methodologically limited. The reporting
is honest and restrained. Tests whether agents can distinguish "weak evidence honestly
reported" (solid) from "strong evidence dishonestly reported" (overclaim). The gold
label is solid because the claims match the evidence quality, even though that quality
has limitations. Expect model disagreement on this case.

## Summary

This text describes a **solid study**. It reports a substantial real-world human trial (2,900 participants, 141 companies, six months) with direct measurement of well-being outcomes. The conclusions stay within the evidence tier—human workers in a real trial reported improved well-being—and the researchers appropriately acknowledge the two main limitations (self-selection bias and self-reported outcomes) while calling for randomized trials as a next step.

The caveats are not decorative; they are substantive and correctly identify the gap between this observational trial and definitive causal evidence. The study is honest about what it can and cannot claim, and the findings are presented in measured language that matches the evidence.
